utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next witness is Dragan Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you make the solemn declaration to speak the truth which reading allowed the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila will now examine you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please tell us your name and profession?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Dragan Milanovic. I have a degree in electrical engineering. I was born in 1951 in Niksic. I completed elementary school in Tuzla, in Bosnia-Herzegovina; high school in Bor; and the Faculty of Electrical Engineering, at the university in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please remove that piece of paper from the desk. You shouldn't have anything on that table. Mr. Milanovic, what did you do from 1995 until 2000? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Elektroistok; that is to say, that is my first and only company for as long as I worked in Yugoslavia, rather, in Serbia. I started in Elektroistok in 1975 as a trainee. During my career, I was promoted all the way up to technical director. This is a company that deals with the transmission of electric energy throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia. It is organised in five - how should I put this? - regional centres. Up until 1998, the end of the summer, that is, I was director of a plant in Bor; and after that, from 1998 to 2000, I was director of Elektroistok; that is to say, this company for power transmission in Serbia, that is to say, the technical director for that for all of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the time of the NATO strikes, were transformer stations and plants NATO targets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Practically, transmission plants, that is to say, transmission lines and transformer stations, were the only target as far as the electric industry is concerned. NATO did not bomb power plants. But as for transmission - and that is really the blood circulation, so to speak, of the entire system - that is what NATO bombed, particularly in May, from the 2nd of May up until the end of May. There were more than nine attacks in two stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the transformer station in Bor? Was it also bombed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Bor has four transformer stations. One is a system-based one of 400 kilowatt, and within it is the regional dispatch centre for regulating electric energy in the area. That is Bor 2. In addition to that, there is a transformer station which has to do with distribution; that is to say for general consumption. That is Bor 1. In Krivelj, there is this transformer station for the mining industry oriented toward the Krivelj mine, and transformer station Bor 3 which is - how should I put this? - in the centre of the foundry of Bor, and its basic purpose is for consumers within the RTB Bor, the mining and foundry complex of Bor. That had been bombed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: It was bombed on the 15th of May around 2200 hours the first time. After that, within four, five-day intervals, it was bombed another two times, so it was practically bombed until it was levelled to the ground. We needed four months only to clear the rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you happen to be when the transformer station Bor 3 had been hit, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Around 8.00, in the evening, I had come from Nis where I had been working all day, where I was organising work in eliminating the effects of the bombing of the transformer station of Nis 2, which is the biggest one in the Balkans. It was bombed with fibre optic shells, and the warehouse of Jugopetrol was bombed on that day. It's 50 metres away from this system-based transformer station that I referred to. Some transmission lines were hit then as well. So Bor had a great many problems in terms of providing power to all our consumers, and they asked me to come from Nis so that we could analyse what the situation was on the ground so that we'd see what it to do. So I arrived from Nis around 8.00 in the evening. I arrived in Bor, and I was at Bor 2 when this strike took place against Bor 3 at 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's not the one that was hit, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm saying this is the system-based transformer station, within which the dispatch centre is, and we were all analysing things as to what could be done if yet another transmission line was to be hit. This system-based trance former station is about ten kilometres away from this other station, Bor 3, that had been hit and that is supposed to provide electricity for the RTB Bor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And why was it you exactly who was working on this there and in other places in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of my position and my knowledge, I was technical director. I had a great deal of experience in maintaining and developing the network. How should I put this? I'm familiar with the soul of the Serbian network. Wherever there were serious problems - and there were quite a few at that - I intervened with my teams throughout Serbia; that is to say, from Vojvodina all the way to the Albania-Macedonian-Bulgarian borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you find out that Bor 3 had been hit? You said you were ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Bor 3 has two feeds from the Bor 2 station. We were sitting there and working, and we heard an explosion from far away. At the same moment, the alarm went off on Bor 2. I looked at the board, and I saw that these two transmission lines that were the feeders of the transformer station were no longer functioning. It was obvious that something terrible had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: At the same moment, I got into the official car, and I went to Bor 3 where I saw that the person who was manning the station had been hit. His arm had been wounded. I took him to hospital. In the meantime, he came to. I handed him over to the doctors. The wound was not that bad. Then, with Ljubo Spasojevic, who was the local director, I went to the transformer station, the transformer station that had been hit, to see what the proportions of the damage were. When I realised what the damage was -- the extent of the damage was, and when I thought what the possible solution might be, I went to RTB Bor and I was sure that I would see the management of the system there. It's a well-known thing in Bor when something happens within the RTB Bor, all the management of the entire system, starting with the foreman upwards, they quickly assemble to see what should be done in order to redress the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And who did you find there at the management building of the Bor company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: In the management building of RTB Bor, that is to say, of the foundry and refinement, I first saw that the lights were on in the director's office and that there were people there. I went there and Nikola Sainovic came up. He came in his car. Inside we found, well, roughly, I think, about 20 people. The general director of Bor, Ninoslav Cvetanovic; then there was the director of a factory, Mirko Grcic; then the director of the foundry, Veselin Savovic; then there was the director of the mining sector, Blagoje Spasovski; then there was the desk officer for protection, Dusko Nikolic; Ljubo Spasojevic, the local director for transmission, was with me. That is to say, there were about 20 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that then Nikola Sainovic came roughly at the same time you did in his own car. Did he drive it on his own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: On his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Without an escort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: He drove his own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see him there on the 15th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't surprised. Nikola Sainovic has close ties to Bor. He was born in Bor. He grew up in Bor, and that is not only characteristic of him being attached to Bor. It's a general characteristic of all of us who spent part of our lives in Bor. We are attached to Bor. Now, Nikola Sainovic is in a bit of a special situation, even in comparison to me. He has a weekend cottage there. He has a mother who is well advanced in age, so he wants to keep her out in the fresh air. He held some very high offices outside Bor; but irrespective of that, he'd always go back to Bor, and he'd find his own peace there, as he puts it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what were the positions he held in Bor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm afraid I'm going to make some mistakes because I really do not belong to that world. I know that he was chief of the local party. He was the local party chief, then he was president of the municipality, then he was -- well, I know more about this now. He was director for the development of RTB Bor, and that is where we had an excellent cooperation. I met him there as an engineer. Then, I think -- no, it's not that I think. I'm sure. Well, I don't know whether there was something in the meantime, but I know for sure, at any rate, that he was Minister for Energy in the government of Serbia. After that, he was Prime Minister of Serbia, and after that the Deputy federal Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was a Member of Parliament as well, wasn't he, I assume, for that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can you help me with what exactly is RTB Bor? When the installations in Bor were described, I think it was simply that these initials were used. It's a mining and foundry complex, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mining and foundry complex of Bor. The witness is an engineer and he worked there, so he can give you the best possible explanation as to what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it comes under the same umbrella as Elektroistok, or is it different from Elektroistok. I think you need to clarify the distinction between these for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic, can you explain to the Chamber what Elektroistok is, where you worked, and what RTB Bor exactly means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: The mining and foundry basin of Bor, RTB - I mean, that's the abbreviation that stands for it - that is a copper manufacturer from the actual copper mine to the final product, all the way up to the final product. Elektroistok, on the other hand, is part of the power industry of Serbia. It includes all the power plants that make power. There is a single company only that deals with the transmission of power, of electric energy, and there are seven or eight companies for -- for the distribution of power; that is to say, that these are two completely independent companies. I worked in the power company, or rather, in the electric energy industry dealing with power transmission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the transformer station of Bor 3 was within the RTB Bor complex; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Physically, it was located within RTB Bor, and it was supposed to provide electricity for the consumers within RTB Bor. In terms of ownership, it belonged to Elektroistok, or rather, the company for transmission, for power transmission, of the Republic of Serbia, because at this transformer station we were practically selling power to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know where Nikola Sainovic had come from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Sainovic was in jeans and he looked sleepy to me, so I thought that he had come from his weekend cottage. Well, this is what I thought and this was my impression, and that proved to be true. As we were walking into the room, we walked in together into this conference room. Mirko Grcic, the director of one sector in Bor, said, "Are you coming from the lake?" And he said, "Well, yeah." And he said, "When did you come?" And he said, "I've been here for a few days now."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "From the lake means," from his weekend cottage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where he has his weekend cottage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he said when he had to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you speak or agree anything about the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: You know, this foundry section of Bor has -- is organised around hot technologies for melting copper, and that's why these -- the purpose of these meetings is to take adequate measures to reduce the damage that would be the consequence of a power failure. And that was the principal topic of the discussions. I tried to introduce another topic to stop, or rather, not to activate, not to use that procedure any more because there was an ecological threat for the entire region. But they were very busy with their own problems, which compressor should be switched on, which should be switched off, et cetera. So, on that evening, I didn't have the chance to speak about what I wanted to discuss. And when we started discussing what to do next, then they called a meeting on the following day, at 10.00 of the following morning, at the municipality president's office. There were many problems again, and I had to go to Novi Sad on the following day. So I left for Belgrade on the spot, and the local director, Ljubo Spasojevic, went to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you said they agreed to meet at 10.00 at the municipality president's office, does that include Nikola Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nikola Sainovic; the director of the mining basin, Ninoslav Cvetanovic; and the municipality president, Ilija Tanikic; and the other managers of the various sections of the mining basin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said, a minute ago, that you returned to Belgrade immediately, and did anyone contact you on the following day around noon on behalf of the municipality president -- or rather, from Zebic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not from Zebic, from Bor. Yes, the municipality president Ilija Tanikic called me. He was a nervous guy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop in advance of that question, Mr. Milanovic. Mr. Fila will now ask you any additional question he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When he called you, was Mr. Sainovic present then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so because they had agreed to meet, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they require you to activate that transformer station, too, and you refused?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, refused would be too harsh a word, but my idea was not to activate the trance former station because the bombers would be back. And I never gave instructions, and I discreetly or tacitly didn't allow that transformer station to be activated again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But irrespective of that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: But after the second wave, and especially third wave of bombers, there was nothing left to activate. As I said, we needed four months just to clean up the debris.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's now tackle another topic, which will also be the last I'll ask you about. During the bombing, you described what you were doing with regard to the transmission network, and you said that NATO bombed with using these special kind of bombs and that their targets were transformer stations. About the damage done, did you contact Nikola Sainovic regarding that during the war in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely speaking, he contacted me. After each bombing - and these were mostly night-time bombings after 9.00 p.m. until dawn - and after these massive attacks, the consequences of which were power failures and blackouts in all of Serbia, he called me on my mobile phone and he wanted to know. That's what impressed me always, and that's why I answered his calls, because I usually didn't answer phone calls at the time. He was interested in whether people had been wounded or whether there were casualties. He didn't ask for details, but he was interested in our forecast with regard to when we could put the plant in function again and which parts of Serbia had been left without power.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you answer the following: How much time had elapsed after the bombings and when he called you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Mobile phones, 15 minutes before the bombing and half an hour after the bombing, did not function. So there was -- the network crashed. So he would call at least half an hour after the bombing. As to from which phones, I'm not sure from which phones he called me, but I know that in my phone's memory I had his home number. And I have already said that due to my many obligations and to the -- to all the communication with regard to putting the system back into function, I didn't answer all calls. I can show you the phone and the entry in my phone read "Saja." And I still know the know the number, and I would answer his calls and tell him what he wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that a Belgrade number?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 011, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that is his home number?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his home number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what you said, but it wasn't recorded. Can you tell us in rough terms how often that happened during the bombing, once, twice, ten times, several times, whatever?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean how often he called me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, he called every time after each bombing. There were some nine attacks. Possibly, he failed to call at one time or another, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the -- whether Nikola Sainovic consulted you at any time with regard to the graphite bomb attacks against the power lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he asked me - I don't remember exactly when it was - a day, two, or three after the first attack with the fibre optics, and that attack was on the 2nd. On the 4th or 5th of May, he asked me on the phone, so it was a very brief conversation. And they -- the weapons used were new. That was a new type of weapon, and it is used for the production of radar screens. And this time it was used to cause short circuits in power plants and installations. And then he wanted to know what we were doing about that, and I answered we remove -- that we removed it mechanically. And I couldn't tell him on the phone with who he were working on the development of a chemical means to turn these fibre optics into -- into non-conducting fibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me put you one last question. How long have you known Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: For 41 years, since 1946 -- sorry, 1966. I came to Bor from Tuzla at the time. I was in second form of secondary school, and he attended technical school at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How would you characterise the man, professionally and as a person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a tough one. There are two aspects to that. I met Nikola Sainovic as an engineer. We've known each other for 41 years, and we socialised and we met each other in town. But for the first time I met him as an engineer was when he was the director of development at RTB Bor. He was an engineer at the time. And I was pleasantly surprised by his profound technical knowledge and even more by his very pragmatic technical logic. At the time, he started something which nowadays is very topical throughout the world, and that is rational power consumption, power economy. And he consulted me with regard to that because we were already engaged in activities concerning the transmission network, and he had a clear vision for that to grow into a section that would deal with the management -- with managing the entire system. And his first step toward registering and recording power consumption had been done. He was an excellent engineer. It's too bad that he was lost for the profession. And the second aspect, you've already asked me what he had done. He was -- he held a number of high positions. With regard to his characteristics as a person, it may be best if I gave you two examples so that you can draw your own conclusions. He was held in high esteem in the environment where he had spent most of his life, but he was also known for the following: It was impossible for him to hire anyone -- anyone if that wasn't strictly in line with the rules, and he wouldn't have a child inscribed in school against the rules. And my opinion was that it wasn't -- that wasn't a good thing, that he was wrong. And he answered to me, "You know, Dragan, the first child I would admit against the rules would not be -- would not only be bad for that child, but it would be even worse for another child who could not be admitted because this kid was admitted against the rules." That -- that's what his personality was like. And something else that I must mention. Those were hard times in Serbia, the embargo, the transition process. They were really hard times, and he was one of the very few people who never had crooks around him. And "crooks" is the term used in civilised countries; and in countries in transitions, you call them tycoons. He never had that sort of people around him. He was a very moral person, very ethical, and he was very demanding toward his fellow workers with whom he communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And with regard to his humanitarian work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: He was not only known for not employing anyone against the rules or admitting anyone to school against the rules. He was also known not only in Bor, but in all of Timocka Krajina, the region surrounding Bor. Whenever he learned that someone was ill or having problems, a child or someone's mother, et cetera, it was certain that that person would be placed in the best hospital and would be provided the best medical carry available. That was a logical consequence of his entire personality. I cannot characterise it as love towards Sainovic on the part of the inhabitants, but they respected him greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milanovic. Thank you for coming here and thank you for these nice words, and now you are the Prosecution's witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked about the role and functions of Mr. Sainovic, and you said that you might make mistakes because you don't really belong to that world. Do you know what his roles and functions were in regard to events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't have the faintest idea. I'm an engineer, a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said that you never knew him to have -- to associate with tycoons and crooks. Do you know whether he's been charged with any criminal offence in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether he was charged. I haven't been in Serbia for two years now. And after the October events, or in other words after the democratic transition of power, there was a massive hysteria about everything that meant -- that had any significance on the technological professional world, and there were also stories in the papers about the head of customs. I remember a man called Zebic, and the name of Nikola Sainovic was also mentioned. I can only say what -- what I heard, and I'm not sure about the source of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Milanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my next witness is Zivadin Jovanovic, the former federal Minister of Foreign Affairs of the former Yugoslavia, and that's likely to take quite some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading allowed the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Fila, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to sit comfortably. This will take some time. For the record, please state your name.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Zivadin Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tell us about your state and party positions, the positions that you held back in 1998 and 1989 -- 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in those years. As for my party positions, I was chairman of Council for International Cooperation Committee of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you become minister in the federal government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1998. I remained in that position until November 2000

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have a diplomatic career before then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a career diplomat. I had worked in diplomacy with almost no interruptions since 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what was the situation in Kosovo and Metohija in the spring and summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was very difficult. There were terrorist activities by a terrorist organisation known as the Kosovo Liberation Army. These activities were continuing and were growing in intensity by the month. The legal [as interpreted] channels were used to bring weapons into Kosovo and Metohija, as well as equipment. The terrorists were attacking members of the authorities; such as the police, the army, members of state services and members of public services and utilities, such as the post, the schools,, regardless of the ethnicity of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there abductions and killings, too?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You might say that the abductions and the killings were more or less a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, just one moment. Line 10, I think the sentence should read "illegal channels," rather than the "legal channels."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you get the binder, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I can see. My apologies. It's an omission on my part, but it's all in my birth certificate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you please open tab 1 and look at document 2D32. As you see, this is a federal document, document of the federal government, and the date is the 25th of March, 1998. So what you're supposed to tell us is this: How did this document come about, and what is it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document shows the positions of the federal government that they sent to the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, after the federal government had reviewed the activities of Yugoslavia's diplomacy with regard to Kosovo and Metohija, and this is something that I presented to the federal government at a previous session. The document shows clearly the method used by the government in its work in the sphere of foreign affairs and foreign relations. It shows that a report on diplomatic activities is submitted to the federal government by the federal minister. The federal government then considers the report and adopts certain positions and certain decisions based on which the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs then acts. In terms of substance, this document says that there is now a more objective approach by international players to problems in Kosovo and Metohija, and that opportunities are being created for further constructive action on the part of Yugoslavia's diplomacy. Furthermore, the document clearly shows that it was the policy of the federal government for all problems to Kosovo and -- in Kosovo and Metohija to be dealt with, at least as far as Yugoslavia's official policy was concerned, by dialogue and political means alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was prime minister at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoje Kontic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And later Momir Bulatovic became prime minister; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. Later on, Mr. Momir Bulatovic became prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were a high-ranking member of that cabinet. Could you please tell us what your position is on this: What was the position of the SFRY government in -- with regard to international integration processes? Were they ready to take up commitments in order to join all these processes and be part of the whole system? Before you answer, please look at 2D55, and that's at tab 2 for you, sir. What sort of a document is this? Who did you send this letter to and why? The letter is at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was federal Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the government strategy was to reintegrate the country, to reincorporate it into all of Europe and world organisations in which the former -- in which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia saw its own interests mirrored. Let me remind you that, at the time, Yugoslavia was under suspension in terms of its membership rights in both the UN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I wonder if you could try to confine your answers to the particular questions you're being asked. This is going to be a very long passage of evidence without really reaching anything as yet that may be of significance to us. And we also have difficulty with the tab itself, Mr. Fila, because what I have at the moment is a letter in French. Was it sent in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking the witness to explain what it is, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, though. We don't have the English. Can you tell us if there's a reason for that? Have we to work in French on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English exists. At least I requested a translation, but the CLSS told me that French, too, was an official language and that they wouldn't translate from French into English. So all we can do is for me to learn English and for you to learn French, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we can proceed in this instance in French. That's your proposal, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But what I can do is ask the witness to read the first paragraph, and he can explain what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any other solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 2D55, that we have both in my binder and in the binder we just received from the Defence, is a one-page document. Now, I hear that we're speaking about page 2 of the document. It's also a document in English. So we have for here 2D55, a one-page document in English, which I think my friend has the answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you see in English is the cover letter, but document itself is in French. Can we please have the following document brought up in e-court, 2D55, and then we'll see. This is the document, and it's in French. It says: "I have the honour of sending to you on behalf of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia the requested admission to the Council of Europe, and I would like to ask you to invite the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in compliance with Article 4 of the Statute of the Council of Europe to join the Council of Europe." It is the meaning of this document to show the efforts being made by Yugoslavia to reactivate its membership in various international organisations. Is it fine now? May I press on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this document is our country's request to become a member of the Council of Europe; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this displays the desire on the part of our country to do just that. In my capacity as federal Minister of Foreign Affairs, and on behalf of Yugoslavia's government, I sent this letter to the Secretary-General of the Council of Europe, followed by my request for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to be admitted as a member to the Council of Europe. The letter says that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is able to take up any responsibility that would stem from its membership in the Council of Europe. It is also specifically emphasised that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will sign and ratify the Council of Europe convention of -- on human rights and the framework convention on minority rights. The letter was dispatched on the 18th of March, 1998. A short while after, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- or rather, its Federal Assembly ratified the Council of Europe convention on minority rights. Another thing you can tell based on this is that the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as far as this request is concerned to be admitted to the Council of Europe, and as far as the convention on minority rights is concerned, the government forwarded these to their field office in Pristina in Kosovo and Metohija, which continued to exist and work throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As terrorist activities intensified in the spring of 1998, how was that reflected on the foreign policy position of Yugoslavia at the time? Just pause between my question and your answer. Yes. Now go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the intensification of terrorist activities in the province of Kosovo and Metohija aggravated and complicated the international position of the country. Pressures were on the rise from different quarters, and also there was a growing need on the part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to objectively portray the situation as it was to its partners in the international field. Primarily, an effort was made on an international level to understand the fact that all the problems in Kosovo and Metohija are derived from separatism and terrorism from Albanian terror structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the Security Council of the UN? Did it adopt a resolution cautioning your country about something?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Security Council adopted several resolutions in relation to Kosovo and Metohija: Resolutions 1160, 1199, 1203, and, finally, 1244.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get to that. Mr. Jovanovic, did you take part in the Milosevic-Yeltsin talks in the autumn of 1998? And you will tell us how it happened that these talks took place and how they evolved, if you were present.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The talks between President Milosevic and President Yeltsin were held in Moscow, if I remember correctly, on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please stop at this point. Open tab 3, 2D -- 2D371, please, and then proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these talks took place at the initiative of President Yeltsin. I think that President Yeltsin, in this particular case, acted on behalf of the international community, which expected an increased international presence in Kosovo and Metohija. In this document, in the joint declaration, it is very important to see that the two heads of state reaffirm the principled position on the necessity of preserving the territorial integrity and respect for the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that they call for a resolution to existing problems through political means on the basis of a full equality of all citizens and all ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there a commitment there to resolve everything through political means?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first subparagraph particularly refers to that; namely, that existing problems would be resolved through political means, respecting the equality of all citizens in all ethnic communities in Kosovo and Metohija; and, in the next subparagraph, that that would be achieved through continuing dialogue, without delay, between the state delegation and the delegation of Albanian political parties. That kicked of with the meeting between President Milosevic and the leader of the Kosovo Albanians, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there anything here that refers to full freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That the FRY is prepared to start talks with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the most important thing that I would like to -- the most important thing for me here is will there be any constraints for foreign diplomatic representatives, in terms of seeing for themselves what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since Yugoslavia encountered certain problems, in terms of understanding problems in Kosovo and Metohija, the Moscow statement accepts international presence through the OSCE; that is to say, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. It was Yugoslavia's interest to have the international community gain direct knowledge through its direct representatives on the ground as to what actual reality was, to gain an objective picture, especially in terms of what the causes were in Kosovo and Metohija; that is to say, of the problems existing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. What was envisaged here, that there would be no restraints in terms of the presence of international observers there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Full freedom of movement was envisaged there for the international representatives and a full openness of the Yugoslav Serbian side to cooperation. This stemmed from Yugoslavia's aspiration to normalise, as soon as possible, its status and its membership in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, where its membership rights had been suspended from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. What did that mean in relation to international presence in Cyprus [as interpreted], in terms of numbers and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It meant that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia accepted several hundred diplomatic representatives of other countries in Kosovo and Metohija. The only restriction was that these should be diplomatic representatives who had previously been accredited as such in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the transcript, it says "Cyprus," and it should be "Kosovo." So could that please be corrected in the transcript. It says "Cyprus."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, was there an increased presence of international diplomatic representatives in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Soon after the Moscow statement, there was an accelerated presence of foreign representatives in Kosovo and Metohija. They were welcome under the name of the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's right, KDOM. Could you please look at the document in tab 4, 2D367. It has to do with the actual numbers of people present. How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that shows that, on the 10th of July, 1998, less than a month from the Moscow joint statement, there were 18 diplomatic representatives of the United States of America in Kosovo and let's, 13 representatives of the Russian Federation, four representatives of Austria, two representatives of Italy, four representatives of Sweden, two from Great Britain, one from the Netherlands, one from Norway, one from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did this number grow eventually?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to indicate that this was just the momentary situation as far as the number of foreign diplomats was concerned in Pristina. From day-to-day it changed; and probably on that day, the day that the report refers to, it was much bigger, if one were to take into account presence in other towns and villages in the province. However, there was a rapid increase in the number in any case, and very soon it ranged in the hundreds. In addition to these foreign diplomatic representatives in the province of Kosovo and Metohija, there were about 400 representatives of the foreign media from all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us now what it was that these foreign diplomats were doing in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the reports that I received from the office of the federal Foreign Ministry in Kosovo and Metohija, I can conclude that foreign diplomats from KDOM primarily had intensive contacts with the representatives of political parties of all the ethnic communities; primarily, the Albanian community, and also with representatives of the local authorities, as well as the representatives of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. In August 1998, did an even bigger number come?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In August 1998, there was an abrupt growth in the number of foreign diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija, and it is my personal opinion that one of the reasons was that the United States of America practically, in that summer of 1998, made a decision to recognise the terrorist KLA as a liberation movement, because high representatives of the American administration started to have public contacts and dialogue; that is to say, relationship of partnership with the representatives and commanders of the terrorist KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All of these diplomatic representatives, the hundreds you refer to, did they tour Kosovo and Metohija 24 hours a day? Did they go all over, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to your own line of work. The situation in Kosovo, as you described it just now and as it was, how did it have an impact on the activity of the federal government and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, the federal government had to discuss problems and questions related to Kosovo and Metohija at its own sessions, at the sessions of working bodies as well, because the situation required that. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What situation? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation of terrorist activity on the rise all the time in Kosovo and Metohija. The permanent increase of attacks that ended tragically, then kidnappings, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what about the international community? Did it step up its own interest in what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. In addition to KDOM, that is to say, diplomatic representatives of other countries and international organisations - and their presence was growing in Kosovo and Metohija all the time - Kosovo and Metohija was increasingly being visited by high representatives of foreign governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please pause there.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government, bearing that in mind, stepped up its own presence there, its direct presence, in addition to the presence of the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, what was all of this like? What did you, as the Foreign Ministry, decide in relation to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In May 1998, I, as federal Minister for Foreign Affairs, decided to open an office of the Foreign Ministry in Pristina, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, that is; and soon after that, offices of the Foreign Ministry in Ranilug, in Kosovska Pomoravlje, and Kosovska Mitrovica. That was necessary both in order to help foreign diplomatic representatives and the representatives of foreign governments who visited Kosovo and Metohija, as well as in order to give professional assistance to the representatives of the local authorities who had not had any experience, of course, in maintaining international contacts, especially such frequent ones as in Kosovo and Metohija at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Jovanovic please have some water, a glass and a pitcher? I don't know why it's not there. Oh, I beg your pardon. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did that outpost function?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The outpost, or outposts to be precise, because there were three of them - our ministry had three such outposts - functioned in accordance with the instructions of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs or the minister himself. Nobody else but the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs was authorised to give instructions for work to these representative offices of the Federal Ministry. They did what I have already described and reported on their activities to the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they report to any other persons?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't report directly to anybody else, but the head office, that is, the Federal Ministry, decided who else in the federal administration or other structures needed to be familiarised with these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said that there were three outposts. Now we seem to have four names. Pristina was one, Kosovska Mitrovica, Kosovsko Pomoravlje, and there is one represented in the transcript as Ranilug. Can you help me identify the three that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranilug is the -- is the seat or the head office of Kosovsko Pomoravlje, which is the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Apart from what you have said, did the federal government do anything else about strengthening its presence in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The federal government established a commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before that, did the federal prime minister do anything?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The federal prime minister decided to dispatch or to send the vice-pm, federal vice-pm, Mr. Nikola Sainovic, to Kosovo. The reason for that being the wish to demonstrate a responsible political attitude to the international community, by sending somebody to the field where the international community was massively present, and that someone was a high government official. The second reason was to demonstrate in this fashion the interest on the part of the federal government in cooperating with international community and its organisations where the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in a restricted position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the beginning of negotiating processes, such as Hill?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Had the negotiating process already begun by that time with Mr. Hill and others?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Negotiations were in process with the representatives of the international community, especially with Ambassador Christopher Hill, about a political solution for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are we referring to the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jovanovic, which position Mr. Sainovic had in the federal government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikola Sainovic was chairman of the Foreign Policy Committee of federal government. That was his permanent position, and it is in this capacity that he chaired that committee. And that committee, which was a standing committee, was drafting proposals for federal government that had a foreign policy aspect and that were put on the agenda of the -- the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the time of Mr. Kontic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sainovic was vice-prime minister and chairman of the foreign policy committee of the government during the -- while Mr. Kontic and Mr. Bulatovic were in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had any responsibility during the negotiations in the framework of the Dayton Accord?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to inform the Court that my relations with Mr. Sainovic were strictly official, and that is why I have known him since the time when I was assistant federal minister. Because starting from 1995, he was intensively involved in all activities regarding the implementation of the Dayton-Paris Accord. In that capacity, I escorted Mr. Sainovic on the occasions of two visits to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was also present on the occasion of talks in 1996 with him, when the first delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina visited the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They were about a hundred strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you -- have there been any other international activities on his part? Do you know anything about his international activities with regard to China, Russia, Arab countries, Israel?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sainovic, who was responsible for foreign policy and foreign economic relations in the federal government, often went on official visits to other countries or international organisations, be it as the head of the Yugoslav delegation or as an escort to the Yugoslav president when he visited other countries. I was in China with him when he -- or rather, when President Zoran Lilic visited China. He was the -- in charge of the talks who were -- that were held parallelly with China during that visit. He also visited countries on several continents, primarily European countries. He visited the EU, and he was accepted everywhere as a highly qualified and responsible person. The results for our country and its policy were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you know that he also visited Arab countries, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, did you take part in the work of the Foreign Policy Committee of the federal government; and if so, since what time? Who chaired that committee? What was -- how did that committee work, and which topics were dealt with?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did take part in the Foreign Policy Committee of the federal government, but not the all the time, because the committee sat every Tuesday because our government was in session on Thursdays. And I also had obligations abroad. That's why I was absent occasionally, but then the deputy federal minister would substitute me. As I said, the committee sat every Tuesday. There was an agenda, and those sessions were chaired by the vice-pm and the head of the foreign policy committee, Mr. Sainovic. Members of the committee would be there and, occasionally, there were also other people invited to the session, depending on the nature of the subject matter discussed. Based on the law -- or rather, that committee was established by -- under a law, and the way -- but it didn't take independent decisions. It only prepared the positions of federal government concerning individual topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So that it was the government that decided based on the proposals of the committee.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do answer one more question for me. What was the -- what were the relations between that committee and the SMIP, which was where you were the boss?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The relations were such as were required for the regular functioning of the institutions of this system. It was a -- these were relations of cooperation where everybody had their authority and their mandate without anyone interfering in the business of the other. There have never been problems in our cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Sainovic also have such a relationship? How would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that our relations were official, but it was a normal cooperative relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So you cooperated. In the summer of 1999 [as interpreted], how did you cooperate?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A correction needs to be made. I said "the summer of 1998." So how did you cooperate at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We attended the meetings of the Foreign Policy Committee or the sessions of our federal government. That was one aspect of the cooperation. Another aspect was a technical cooperation. In between sessions and meetings when Mr. Sainovic felt he needed to consult us, we would have a meeting either in my office or his.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we conclude that due to the fact that his position and his obligations were of a foreign policy character, and you also work in the field of foreign policy, did you -- you had to cooperate and your activities were complementary?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is normal for officials, members of government, who cover such wide areas as foreign policy, it is normal that they cooperate. In this long-standing cooperation with Mr. Sainovic, I -- my overall conclusion or impression was that he was a serious politician and a person who responsibly deals with every task assigned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it mean that he worked in accordance with the instructions received from federal government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My mandate was defined by the law, and I was autonomous to a degree, but I was also tied by the strategy and the decisions of government. Mr. Sainovic was responsible for foreign policy in that government, and it is natural that he worked exclusively based on the decisions and positions and the set policy of federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of relationship existed between vice-pm Sainovic and the outpost of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no problems in that relationship. Everybody did their work; and, at the same time, cooperation was normal. The outposts assisted in preparing the meetings that Mr. Sainovic had in the field, either with representatives of the foreign diplomatic mission KDOM or with representatives of members of foreign governments or international organisations. The outposts also reported to the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs of these activities in the field. When necessary, those outposts provided logistical and professional, that is, diplomatic assistance, to Mr. Sainovic. He did not give instructions to those outposts because the heads of the outposts were responsible exclusively to the Federal Ministry; that is, me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the state's reaction to the escalating terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes without saying, I suppose, that it did what any responsible country would do when facing the problem of terrorism. The state had no choice but to defend law and order. It had to defend the constitution. It had to make sure that all citizens were safe in Kosovo and Metohija, and it had to apply force in combatting terrorism. On the other hand, the state used diplomacy in a bid to explain to international players how serious the problem of terrorism had become. It also had to seek understanding for its policy of dealing with the Kosovo and Metohija problem by political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the state try to negotiate with the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did; however, not with the terrorist faction. It tried to hold talks with their political parties, rather, their representatives, the political parties of the Albanian national minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the summer of 1998? As far as you know, was an anti-terrorist operation launched at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did it end and when?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist operation was ended by crushing the terrorist cells and by stifling any activity, terrorist activity, on the part of the Kosovo Liberation Army all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may be a good time for our break since I'm now about to move on to a different subject altogether, the work of the Federal Assembly, that sort of thing. Therefore, I don't think I could possibly deal with that sort of thing in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Jovanovic, we have to break at this stage. That break will about for about half an hour. The usher will take you from the courtroom and show you where to wait while we have this break. Thank you. We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, could you please go to tab 5, document 2D67.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the conclusions of the Federal Assembly, dated the 5th of October, 1998. This is about the circumstances prevailing in Kosovo and Metohija. This also contains a platform to deal with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there anyone who previously adopted these conclusions and then tabled them to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly adopted these conclusions at the proposal of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Adopted them how?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At a joint session of the Council of Citizens and the Council of the Republics, and they were adopted by a unanimous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 2, or item 2, of these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Item 2 comprises the basic elements necessary to deal with the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. They are as follows: "Dialogue as the only way to peaceful and democratic settlement of the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. "Respect for the territorial intaking by of the sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. "A solution harmonised with the constitutions of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and international standards in the area of human and civil rights and the rights of members of ethnic minorities. "Full equality for all citizens and all ethnic communities ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can read this, Mr. Jovanovic. We really need your personal knowledge on particular issues which Mr. Fila will focus; indeed, not only can we read it, but we've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Item 3, please don't read it, Mr. Jovanovic. We can read it ourselves; therefore, it shouldn't being a problem. But tell us the meaning behind item 3, the conclusion in item 3.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The meaning is a warning about the final objective of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, which is political terrorism, and is aimed at breaking up the political and territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the last item?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last item states that "the security forces took measures in the proportion necessary to isolate and eradicate terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Look at item 5, for example. Does the document actually say that the anti-terrorist operation eventually led to a defeat of the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the first two words in item 5. Does it not state that the terrorists were defeated?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to item 11 now, please. What is the Federal Assembly supporting in item 11?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Assembly supports the proposal of the federal government and of the Russian Federation, to invite the OSCE to come to Kosovo and Metohija and start monitoring the situation from close up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So much for that document. Could you please tell us what the international position was of our country, Yugoslavia, in the autumn of 1998, specifically in the month of October?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The position was an exceptionally difficult one. Terrorism had come back to life and had escalated. There was also intense pressure and open threats being made to the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by certain countries, and by NATO specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were these threats about? What did they say would happen?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was an open threat of armed aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is when the so-called "act order" was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did this crisis draw to a close?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: By political agreement between President Milosevic and the envoy of the American president, Mr. Richard Holbrooke, on the 12th of October, 1999 -- 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the role of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in overcoming this crisis and in dealing with the threats at that you mentioned in October 1998? What did the Ministry of Foreign Affairs do specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs stepped up its diplomatic activity in relation to all the key international players, by emphasising the commitment of the federal government to a peaceful and political solution to the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija. This it said should be achieved by dialogue, by equal rights for all citizens and all ethnic minorities. Another thing that was emphasised was the danger and unacceptable nature of any threat, especially that of armed aggression, since threats of that nature are contrary to international law, contrary to any peaceful solution of any problem, and eventually contrary to the Charter of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you do anything about this personally? Did you get in touch with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Following the agreement between President Milosevic and Richard Holbrooke, I, on behalf of the federal government, signed an agreement to establish an OSCE verification mission with the president of the OSCE at the time. This was the Polish Foreign Minister, Mr. Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please look at 2D78. What is that about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is about a session of the federal government, at which I submitted a report about the report of the Secretary-General, the UN Secretary-General, concerning the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. One thing I would like to point out is that this was a preliminary analysis on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the proposal adopted at this government session, the proposed agreement with the OSCE, the one that you had signed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to tab 8, P432, and tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of the agreement on the verification mission. I signed this and Mr. Geremek signed this, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this is what you've been telling it us about; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now explain what the motives were for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to conclude an agreement of this nature?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first and fundamental principal motive was to ensure a diplomatic presence in Kosovo by an international agency so that the international community could see for itself what the situation was in Kosovo and Metohija. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had no reason to conceal anything concerning the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. Quite the contrary in fact. Yugoslavia wanted the international public to get an unbiased idea about what was happening in Kosovo and Metohija. The other thing was to open some form of cooperation with the international community. That was the intention of the federal government to deal with the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. The third thing was to express an interest on the part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in normalising its rights as a member of the OSCE through this cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at the preamble to this agreement, please, the agreement on the OSCE verification mission.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The preamble states the basic principles and the initial positions expressed by the parties to the agreement, respect to the principles of the UN Charter and of the Helsinki final act. The other principle mentioned is for all problems to be solved based on the equality of all citizens and ethic communities, to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states in the region, and to consistently implement Resolutions by the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There is really no need to go through the specific wording. We just need your comment. Do we see official name of the province being used in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the only international document using the name of Kosovo and Metohija as it was under the constitution, the province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Could you now go to section 1, item 5, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this item, the two parties agree that the KVM would replace KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And there would be some integration; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. KVM would absorb KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that ever carried through?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Never, never carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 6 now. What is it that the government of -- takes upon itself to do?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Proceeding from the fact that this is a diplomatic mission, and in keeping with the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations, the safety and security of the KVM and its members shall be guaranteed exclusively and only by the government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the first part in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's right. The government of Serbia will receive the OSCE mission. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 reaffirms the joint desire of the signatories of this international agreement; namely, that the members of the verification mission will enjoy all rights and carry out their obligations in accordance with the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That practically means that every member of the verification mission would be treated as a foreign diplomatic representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. We know the rest. Could you please -- oh, well, all right. I've dealt with all of that. Could you please look at the second part now, and then there's a paragraph 1 there as well. It refers to reports to the OSCE, to the Security Council, and other organisations. It says: "The verification and implementation of the Resolution," and so on and so forth. That's how it starts. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Over here I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Look at the Serbian version; don't look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but in the English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. The Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it's not in the right order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English version, that's for the Court. It's page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The beginning of the sentence is "to verify compliance," et cetera. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of the English version?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: English version. What was the paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 1, the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Wait a minute. We know how to read. We see what's there. Does it say here that reports would be submitted -- well, to who will the reports be submitted? That's what matters.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This provision envisages the obligation of the KVM to send its report to its headquarters in Vienna, that is to say, the OSCE, but to submit them along parallel lines to the government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they submit at least one report to you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Not a single KVM report was ever submitted to the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was never any explanation, but there were requests from the Yugoslav side. Inter alia, I asked Knut Vollebaek, the chairman in office of the OSCE, and he promised me to look into the matter. He said that the Yugoslav side would be receiving reports, but that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at part III, paragraph 1 now. The name of part III is "Specific terms of reference."

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what is stated there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, this envisages that the KVM would have freedom of movement throughout Kosovo and easy access.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does that mean? How do you interpret that? What is that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a language expert; but as a party, as a signatory to this agreement, my understanding was that this means freedom of movement throughout the territory of the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And access to various localities, that no parts of the territory were off limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the transcript -- oh, it's been corrected. Part of the witness's answer was recorded as a question, but now it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
