utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'd like to ask you something else now in relation to this. It does have something to do with this. In international practice, according to your many years of experience, is there any difference between freedom of movement and access and arms control?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, there's a difference, and these are completely separate categories. Freedom of movement is a concept that is used frequently in all international documents; whereas, arms control is regulated by special sui generis agreements because, among other things, it requires specialists for the field of arms control, and it requires special procedures that are regulated very specifically in very specific international documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, as one of the two signatories, you are one of the signatories and the other one is Mr. Geremek - and we haven't had the honour of hearing him - could you tell me whether in this agreement of yours between you and Mr. Geremek? Is there any reference to arms control?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "arms control"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just gave an answer to the question put by the Defence whether there is a distinction between freedom of movement and arms control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand you've answered that question. What I'm asking you is what is "arms control"? What do you mean by that expression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there are different international documents about arms control in the fields of classical, nuclear, and other arms. I know that there are also specific agreements on regional arms control in the territory of the former SFRY, and I know, as a layperson, that this control can be exercised by specialists, according to specially regulated procedures. And I know that, in my view, this control cannot be carried out by civilian persons and unqualified diplomats, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps we are going to get there now. Please look at 21011.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Now something like NPT, Nuclear Proliferation Treaty, would you take it as an arms control treaty? Is it in that nature that you're talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am just stating that such agreements do exist. On the basis of the experience I have, I know that arms control is a complex process that requires special knowledge and special procedures. As for the content of these procedures, I am not familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, let me try to be of assistance. Mr. Jovanovic, you and Mr. Geremek, did you talk about arms control at all, about entering barracks, counting cannons, guns, what have you? Did you discuss that at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now look at tab 12. The document is 2D11. It exists only in the English language. Could you please interpret it for us. Could you please tell us what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an agreement. It is the Agreement on Subregional Arms Control that was signed in Florence. It shows that a special protocol was signed pertaining to arms control only.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the FRY; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All countries of the subregion, including the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As for the implementation of that agreement, there were never any problems, not on any side, including the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this agreement also signed under OSCE auspices?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page of this document, and we can see who signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: Does this agreement envisage the possibility of inspecting arms in the region, including the FRY, at any point in time, whenever necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This agreement was fully implemented. For years it has been archived now as something that has already been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia abide by this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for the attitude of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia vis-a-vis this agreement, there were never any objections from any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know about inspection requests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop, please. There was a question there not answered. At page 49, line 1: "My question is: Does this agreement envisage the possibility of inspecting arms in the region, at any point in time, whenever necessary?" And there's no answer to that question. What would your answer be to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement signed in Florence in 1996 was fully carried out. Every one of the signatories fully met its obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not understand my question, Mr. Jovanovic? It was Mr. Fila's question, not mine, but the question was: Did the agreement envisage the possibility of arms inspections being carried out, at any point in time, whenever necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As for inspection requests, and even unannounced inspections, in accordance with this agreement, were they all carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the implementation of this agreement, all requests put forth by the parties, the signatories, were accepted and carried out in good faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're obviously at cross-purposes here. I would find it very difficult to know what is the relevance of the implementation of an agreement in relation to Bosnia, in relation to the case we're dealing with here. It's an entirely collateral issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way it would be if it pertains to Bosnia, but it pertains to Yugoslavia. If you look at the document, that means that the verification of all the armed forces of Yugoslavia was carried out, as well as the in the other regions. It's a subregional agreement. It applies to the entire subregion. There were unannounced checks, inspections, in barracks and other military localities. According to this agreement signed in Florence in 1996, it meant that there would be arms control and there would be checks as to whether we had an atomic bomb or what have you not. So that applies to Yugoslavia and to the entire subregion. It will pertains to all countries of the region, all countries of the former Yugoslavia, the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jovanovic, whether inspections were carried out in Kosovo in terms of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, announced or unannounced, inspections could be made at any point in time, by any one of the parties, in any part of the territory of any one of the signatories; that is to say, that inspections could be carried out in the province of Kosovo and Metohija as well. However, I hope that you will understand me. I'm not a specialist in arms control, and I really would not be the right person to talk to in relation to specific subjects from this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise. But you can tell us about the purposes and the rationale behind this; no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question from this field.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, no, no. Since we've been dealing with your agreement, with Geremek, that's what we're going to talk about throughout. How do you assess some requests by some verifiers that the Geremek -- that according to this Geremek-Jovanovic agreement, they carry out verification of arms in Kosovo and Metohija because they had -- or rather, did they have the right to that or not according to your agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement that I signed with the chairman in office of the OSCE, Mr. Geremek, does not contain in any one of its provisions any grounds for arms control or the control of military equipment in any part of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you envisage verification of the forces and weapons to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not understand the question in terms of what provision it applies to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intend to go on dealing with this agreement. I'm going to continue along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at section III, the specific terms of reference, in paragraph 1, what you agreed on was the verification of the maintenance of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was agreed upon, and that was one of the objectives of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the cease-fire involve the withdrawal of any forces from Kosovo and a limitation on the number of forces that should be in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my negotiations with Mr. Geremek, and in the agreement, there was no mention of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had that already been agreed by someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Maybe it would be useful for me to repeat this once again. Did you and Mr. Geremek discuss arms at all, the control of barracks, the counting of soldiers? Did you deal with military matters at all? Because it says here that you -- that the parties abide by the cease-fire. That means that if someone shoots, what happens?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, the text of the agreement that was signed is clear, precise, and fully self-explanatory. The agreement clearly shows what the issues were that we as foreign ministers discussed and what it was that we agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on. Please look at tab 8. P432 is the number of the document. It's the same tab that you have there. Now I'd like to look at section 4, paragraph 2. What is envisaged here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The minister and the chairman in office of the OSCE, that is to say, Mr. Geremek, and I agreed --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the Judges are conferring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 4. Paragraph 4 and then subparagraph 2. It says: "It will be allowed," et cetera. What does this say?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a provision stating that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia agrees to accept a diplomatic civilian mission consisting of 2.000 persons with diplomatic status.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Something else is written after "2.000."

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian diplomatic representatives who are to be treated in accordance with the Vienna Conventions on diplomatic relations, and it is stated specifically that none of the members can be armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So who would be responsible for their safety and security then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The parties to the agreement agreed that as far as safety and security is concerned of this civilian unarmed mission that it would be guaranteed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the receiving country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, how many verifiers arrived in Kosovo and Metohija in total?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Their largest number was 1.300 just before their withdrawal from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at paragraph 6 of section IV.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a provision pertaining to equipment that the diplomatic mission would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It envisages what?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Vehicles, communications, and other equipment, along with local staff for administrative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Did you find anywhere in this agreement something stating that they have the right to use their own helicopter?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for me to look. There is no such provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, weren't we asked that the mission should be allowed to use a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The position of the federal government was that, in case a helicopter should be needed, the government would place its own helicopter with crew at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And why were they not given one then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There are two reasons: One, this is not in line with the agreement; two, because it is safer and more practical to have helicopters from the host country flying over its territory, and thus to guarantee for the safety of the flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So we can see that there was some demands which, according to you and also according to the language of the agreement that you signed, were not covered by the agreement: Entering barracks, counting tanks, helicopter personnel, arms, et cetera. Why did they make such demands?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This could be best explained by those who made such demands. As for me, I think that such demands were commented extensively in the media and tensions were raised, in my opinion, unnecessarily, because this wasn't about a different interpretation of the provisions of the agreement signed but about demands going beyond the agreement. While this was reported about extensive in the media, in the field the terrorism was thriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look again, please, at section III and paragraph 1, could you read the first sentence, please? Just read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The verification mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jovanovic, there is a reference there to a cease-fire. What were the terms of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot provide an answer to that question, because simply I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How, then, can you interpret the rest of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The inspectors, the verification mission, shall have the right to receive reports and probably draft their own reports about the cease-fire, and they can move freely throughout Kosovo at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you may have forgotten something. Did -- was your agreement with Geremek was based on the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was anything agreed in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was agreed that the mission, verification mission, in Kosovo and Metohija should be continued, and this is reflected in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you agree that your agreement is a continuation of the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's an implementation of that agreement in its specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you agreement with me when I say that you, as one of the authors of this text, is in a position to interpret it and to interpret your purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the signatories are in a position to interpret the agreement, but I repeat that the issue is not different interpretations of the agreement but demands going beyond the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Being here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement lead to a determination of the number of VJ forces and MUP personnel in Kosovo, or was that some later agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present at the talks between Milosevic and Holbrooke. With Prime Minister Bulatovic, on the 11th of December, I was in Antalya at the South-East European Summit. But I know that agreement was reached about the establishment of a verification mission, and I talked about that and eventually signed an agreement with Minister Geremek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, did one of your witnesses actually present us with a copy of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were unable to find it, so we couldn't show that it really exists as a signed agreement, but you can trust me that I did everything I could to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you apparently don't know the terms of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for sure that the -- the signing of the agreement about the verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija was agreed upon; and as Minister of Foreign Affairs, I spoke about the content of that agreement with Minister Geremek and signed this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can't tell us anything about the question whether there was agreement reached on numbers of forces and the terms of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain that at the time when President Milosevic and Ambassador Holbrooke had their talks, I was outside Yugoslavia at the South-East European Summit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We understood that, but the Judge wanted to know something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that, but how was it you could go ahead and enter an agreement with Geremek without knowing the terms of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm responsible for the activities of diplomacy, and that is included in the agreement that was signed. In other talks -- or rather, I didn't take part in other talks; and out of respect toward this institution, I do not dare to give interpretations based on second-hand knowledge. I read about the political agreement on a peaceful solution was reached, and that a verification mission should be established, which later on, indeed, was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jovanovic, that General Perisic and General Clark also signed something based on that agreement about -- something about troops?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was informed that some agreement was signed, but I was the not involved so I could not talk about that first-hand, the way I can about facts where I immediately took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us return to other things then. So demands were made for things that were not covered by the agreement, and -- but they did not provide reports as they were -- as they should have under the agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they, at any given time, want the agreement to be amended, enabling them to carry personal arms and using their own helicopter, et cetera? Did you ever receive such requests?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And let us now move on to legal matters. Who was it on the Yugoslav side provided interpretation of the Geremek-Jovanovic agreement, in the case of discord regarding the scope of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The signatories are authorised to interpret the agreement. Talking about Yugoslavia, this is the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs and federal government, but I have already said that interpretation was never an issue. The issue were demands going beyond the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your statement that these were demands going beyond the scope of the agreement, is that your personal opinion or is that also the position of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the position of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs and also my personal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the position of the government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That position was also verified and confirmed by federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at tab 9, document 2D81. Tab 9. Let me now first point to a -- to a translation error, because it says it's a document dated 16th of May 1998. In fact, it's a document dated 16th of October. Please bear that in mind. This is a document that you forwarded to federal government. What can be concluded from this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document shows the procedure of work at federal level, and the relations between the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the federal government. The Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs submitted the signed agreement to the federal government, requesting the government to forward that document to all other line ministries for the purpose of implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was implementation slow or fast?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This shows that the document was submitted to federal government on the day it was signed, from which it follows that Yugoslavia as a state was -- took a great interest in a fast implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to -- what I would like to show to the witness is on the first and only page of the English translation, and it's the last two -- last two paragraphs of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does the Federal Ministry suggest in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As reflecting our responsible attitude towards the implementation of this agreement, our ministry proposed to federal government to urgently establish a Commission for Cooperation with the KVM, and the chairman of that commission should be the vice-pm, Mr. Nikola Sainovic. This is also proposed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you think -- when I say "you," - I don't mean you personally; I mean the minister and the whole Ministry of Foreign Affairs - why did you think that this was necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The answer is also contained in page 1 of the document, from which it could be seen to who the agreement was forwarded. For the purpose of coordination and more efficient cooperation, we needed a commission composed of the representatives of all services charged with the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the rules of procedure of government have -- play any role in that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is also important that under the law two types of -- two types of bodies in government are envisaged by the law: Standing bodies and provisional bodies such as the Commission for the Cooperation with the KVM, which I proposed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you think that Mr. Sainovic should have chaired that commission? Why did the ministry hold this position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because vice-pm Nikola Sainovic was the representative of federal government with the greatest experience in international cooperation, disregarding the Foreign Ministry; because he was accepted as the partner of foreign governments and international organisations; and because I wanted to show to the international community what -- how great an importance the government attributes to cooperation with the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 10, 2D8. What is this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the decision of the federal government to set up a Commission for Cooperation with the KVM. You can see that the chairman is Mr. Nikola Sainovic, and you can see who the members are -- or rather, the relevant ministries represented in the work of this committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean your proposal was accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at line 1 of the new page, the reference to "KLA," I think, should be "OSCE."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please go to tab 11, 2D9, and explain what it's about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the federal government to supplement the composition of the Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE, the OSCE verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You've said this a number of times already, so please be brief. Can you tell us what the position was of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia that the OSCE mission that just arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was one of constructive cooperation. The general mood was for the mission to succeed as envisaged in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Both Yugoslavia's and Serbia's interests coincided in this case; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to tab 14, document 2D318.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the established form for recording important agreements reached with any international representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. If you go to paragraph 1, what does it say? How would you define that? Is this the policy of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are talks at a very high level, high-level talks, during which the deputy prime minister puts forward the fundamental elements of the government policy to deal with problems in Kosovo and Metohija. He also talks about what the prerequisites are for a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 15 now, 2D87. Can you look at the assessments in the last paragraph, please. Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the exhibit is 2D87.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 15 is the -- all right. I apologise. This is a report of the OSCE technical mission at a time when the verification mission was just about to be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what is the assessment? Is it a positive one or a negative one?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's favourable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In relation to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the preparation and the conditions offered by the federal government to the mission and its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you now please go to tab 16, 2D321.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document about the substance of the talks between Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic and Wolfgang Petritsch, the Austrian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the position expressed by Mr. Petritsch, in relation to assessment of the situation previously put forward by Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Petritsch's reaction is favourable, his reaction to the assessments presented by Mr. Sainovic and the talks themselves. When the talks were drawing to a close, he also asked the federal government to continue to demonstrate understanding for the ECMM mission in Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Sainovic did not instantaneously meet Mr. Petritsch's request, but he did say that he would confer with the Foreign Ministry, the federal Foreign Ministry, and that he would probably later be in a position to make public their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what was their position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a reserved one, which you can see on the face of this document. The problem being parallel action by a number of different missions during the existence of the verification mission. It was our belief that all of these different missions would be absorbed into the OSCE operation, including the ECMM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So your position was different, right, from the opinion expressed by the Foreign Ministry?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Foreign Ministry position and my private position, if you like, was this: Regardless of any other interests involved -- or rather, regardless of the desire for there to be just a single mission in Kosovo, this being the OSCE mission, the federal government should still agree to have these two missions go on in parallel, as it were: The ECMM and the OSCE. This was the position of the federal ministry, and the government accepted this; therefore, the ECMM, led by the German ambassador, Mr. Hartwig, continued to operate in parallel with the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please go to tab 17 now, 2D105.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 17, you said; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. 2D105 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Which section?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Halfway through paragraph 1, where the moves of the Yugoslav side are mentioned, what does that tell you? Could you first read it and then comment, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you talking about the notes of the meeting between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. 2D105 is the Foreign Ministry local office in Pristina, confidential meeting between Skoric, deputy head, and Riccardo Sessa, the Italian ambassador. Could you go halfway through the first paragraph. It talks about the moves made by the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This talks about the constructive approach taken by the Yugoslav side towards the international community. In this specific case, we are looking at the requests made by the Italian ambassador, Riccardo Sessa. It is stated here that there is a continued great readiness to work together with the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Same document, paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is the Italian ambassador, Mr. Sessa, expressing his surprise at the statement made by the OSCE president, Mr. Geremek, to the effect that March 1999 will be decisive for the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Geremek got this information?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is his own colleague, the Italian Ambassador Sessa, disagreeing with him, clearly realising that the statement made by Geremek was counter-productive. And this statement came at the very start of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Bearing all this in mind, I can only agree with the reaction expressed by the Italian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Could you please go to tab 18 now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there some other evidence of this statement being made or is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just that. This is the only thing we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we believe is indicative is that they say March, of all months. I think that might start us thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to tab 18, 2D106.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a note to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from Pristina, to the effect that Ambassador Walker, head of the Kosovo Verification Mission, was requesting a meeting with President Milosevic. This shows you the technical side of how meetings were organised between the head of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the state's highest ranking dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What you mean is that the local offices of the Foreign Ministry were used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That was perfectly within their remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you go to tab 19 now, please, 2d119. This is another note on talks between Ambassador Veljic from the under-chiefs of the Federal Customs Administration at the Pristina airport. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is how technical administration and other issues were dealt with, and that's what the document shows, issues that needed dealing with in order to facilitate the Kosovo Verification Mission arrival in Kosovo and Metohija. Another thing that one can see is that all of the agencies having anything at all to do with the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission are parties to these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. Could you please go to tab 20 now. That's Defence Exhibit 2D323. Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go to page 2, please, paragraph 1 specifically. This is paragraph 1 on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, paragraph 2. You mean the second paragraph down the page on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but please look at the first paragraph in Serbia. And in the English document, the paragraph I'm talking about is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document about a meeting between Mr. Nikola Sainovic and the head of the Belgrade OSCE office, Mr. Pellnas. The office was established in line with the agreement, and what brought this meeting about what a protest by a representative -- the deputy prime minister of the federal government to the head of the OSCE mission about the wounding of policemen on the 20th of -- on the 12th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what did Mr. Pellnas say about this? What was his general attitude about this protest?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pellnas, in general terms, expressed his understanding and his regret about the incident. He realised that the protest was more than justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please go to tab 21 now; Defence Exhibit 2D347.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is one of the communiques about a whole series of talks that Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic held with the American ambassador, Chris Hill. They talked about the political solution to the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija. What we see reiterated here is the generally known position of the federal government that the situation could only be dealt with by renewing political dialogue and not by any other means. It is underlined that everyone, and particularly the most influential international players, must condemn terrorism in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please go to tab 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the date on this accurate, the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is out of sequence from the rest of the material, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Just this one. Just this one, and the next one will re-establish the continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 22 now. This is 2D363. This document is in English.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another communique, a press release, about one of the meetings from a series of talks that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic held with the American ambassador, Chris Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The month is November; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 27th of November, 1998. But there were many such meetings that were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And Sainovic appears to be saying what?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that Mr. Sainovic and the federal government are concerned that too much tolerance is being displayed vis-a-vis the terrorist activities. One thing I wish to underline is that in the period, between October and December 1998 alone [Realtime transcript read in error "December 1998"], there were over 500 terror strikes in Kosovo and Metohija, and we are talking about only as many as two months of the Kosovo Verification Mission being present in the area, yet there were over 500 terrorist strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you go to tab 23 now please. This is Defence Exhibit 2D196, item 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the period you stated for over 500 terror strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, over 500 terrorist strikes occurred in October, November, and December 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript simply reflected December for some reason, and I thought I heard October to December. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you found tab 20, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you go to paragraph -- or item 2, paragraph 2, and the first paragraph on page 2. Sainovic appears to be saying something about the normalisation, about restoring normal relations. Can you explain what that is about. This is the bottom of page 1 and the top of page 2 of the English version of the report.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I wish to draw your attention to the kind and level -- the nature and legal of these talks. What we see here is deputy prime minister and the vice-president of the European Commission talking. The federal policy is here reaffirmed about the need of restoring relations between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one hand and the EU on the other. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is an integral part of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 24. This is Defence Exhibit 2D169. This is a document about Ms. Sadako Ogata's visit to Yugoslavia. Could you please go to the second paragraph and tell us what Ms. Sadako Ogata said about this visit.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the Foreign Ministry for the benefit of the federal government. In addition to other things, it shows that Ms. Sadako Otaga toured quite a number of different places in Kosovo and Metohija. She subsequently arrived at the conclusion that the number displaced persons had decreased, and that one could not speak of a humanitarian disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The date on this document, can you tell us the date on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 5th of January. Her visit had taken place between the 20th and the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is now time for our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we will break for an hour at this time. Again, would you please go with the usher, and we will see you again at 1.45. [The witness stands down]. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you rested?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, one physical effort after this break, please look at tab 25, Exhibit number 2D9, I believe, and please look halfway through the second paragraph. What is this about -- Sorry. It's 2D15. 2D15.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document about the talks of Nikola Sainovic with the speaker of Austrian parliament, Hans Fischer, and the vice-pm of Austria, Wolfgang Schussel, held on the 4th of July 1999. The paragraph you're mentioning says that both partners agreed on the necessity of finding a political solution that respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. They also agree that it is necessary to urgently launch negotiations certainly before coming spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a high-level of conversation and do the other participants accept his position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is a high-level conversation. The speaker of parliament receives officials of comparable level, and the Austrian vice-pm, Wolfgang Schussel, is the partner to the vice president of president -- sorry, vice-pm of Yugoslavia. Mr. Schussel is now prime minister of Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they agree on the issues?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They agreed on the principles underlying a solution to the Kosovo Metohija problem, and these principles are on now and needn't be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the top of page 2 of this document. It -- it is also at the top of page 2 of the English translation. What does Sainovic state here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of the conversation, this part of the document, the principles of solving the Kosovo and Metohija problem are pointed out: Respect for the territorial integrity and sovereignty and the principle of the equality of all the ethnic groups and all citizens irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. Mr. Sainovic went to visit an influential country, a member of the European Union, and in which country there -- several international organisations have their headquarters, including the OSCE. He went there to seek the support of such an influential country to a political solution and support for and an urgent continuation of dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he get that support?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document shows that the reactions of the high officials of Austria were positive, and that they even promised they would strive to win over the representatives of Albanian political parties to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go to tab 26 now; Exhibit 2D181.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document about my conversation with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway and the then new chairman in office of the OSCE, Mr. Knut Vollebaek, who had taken over that position in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 1 on page 1. It's also paragraph 1 of the English version. Could you comment, please. What do you speak about here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Two objectives -- there were two objectives of Yugoslav policy: One, for -- that the OSCE mission in Kosovo be successful; and secondly, that the position of Yugoslavia and the OSCE be normalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go to page 2, paragraph 2. It is paragraph 3 on page 2 of the English translation. My question is: Does this contain any remarks about or objections to the activities of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vollebaek asked for a flexible attitude of the Yugoslav side regarding demands about using a Swiss helicopter in Kosovo and Metohija, and to allow personal weapons for bodyguards of the KVM, also, granting the permission for the operation of a radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was your attitude?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My position was that we wanted cooperation with the OSCE, understanding and good relations, but a prerequisite for all of that is honouring the agreement between Yugoslavia and the OSCE. The demands put forward by Mr. Vollebaek went beyond the agreement that was reached, and I asked him to reconsider the offer of the Yugoslav government to put at their free disposal a helicopter of the Yugoslav government. I was saying to him that this was best for the mission because our crews were familiar with the area and capacities could also be strengthened, if necessary. I said to him that we had to bear in mind our goal; namely, to provide a helicopter for transportation in urgent situations, and the Yugoslav side was willing to do so, regarding the helicopter. About weapons for bodyguards, I reminded him that it was very difficult for us to give up the principle that the Yugoslav government guaranteed for all KVM members, including Mr. Walker, and that there was no need to insist on this and create problems where there are no problems. There is a general rule applying to diplomats, and this was a diplomatic mission, and that rule is that security is guaranteed by the host country and not by countries or organisations that send diplomats elsewhere. As for the radio station, I must say I was surprised by this request. At the time in Kosovo and Metohija, there was a practically unlimited number of radio stations and printed media, especially in Albanian. These printed media had an overall annual circulation of two million, and it was not in keeping with the nature of the mission to have an own public media.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it part of the agreement between you and Geremek to allow them to use their own radio stations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were allowed to use means for communication, internal means of communication, and between them and their headquarters in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what did you say was the circulation of the printed media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The circulation of the printed media in Albanian was two million per annum, the total, and none of these media were funded or under any influence of the authorities. On the contrary, all those were mildly speaking oppositional media, media that publicly advocated activities directed against the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was just that it seemed such a low figure that I thought I should clarify it, but it was what you apparently said the first time as well. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I would like to draw attention that circulation of media in Serbia are relatively low, comparing -- compared to those in West European countries, and in Kosovo and Metohija in particularly. As I mentioned, those were exclusively private medias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And let me tell you -- or rather, let me ask you, how many -- what's the rate of illiteracy in our country.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an expert in that field, but illiteracy is, unfortunately, much higher than in Western Europe, but I cannot mention any precise figure because I would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the third paragraph on page 2 of this document. Mr. Vollebaek is informing you about something here. It's the fourth paragraph in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, it is page 2. Vollebaek speaks about --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vollebaek thanked the representative of the federal government for his -- for their attitude, for their restrained attitude, after the kidnapping of eight VJ members, saying that the KVM would become operational only in January 1999, which, in my opinion, was rather late. And this -- it was a detrimental deferring of this, their mission, because the KVM was only established three months after the signing of my agreement with Mr. Vollebaek. There was pressure exerted on the Yugoslav side, and we were urged to sign the agreement as soon as possible. But once the agreement was signed, we were confronted with an unreasonably slow completion of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it our fault for -- that they were organising so slowly?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Clearly, the Yugoslav party isn't to blame for that in any way. The statement of Mr. Vollebaek can be understood in such a way that the OSCE was unable to complete their mission by -- or rather, to make the mission fully operational in late January. And as late as March, two-thirds of its staff were not yet in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let us, please, look at page 2 and -- which is toward the end of the English version.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me point toward the wish of Yugoslavia at the time to live up to all its obligations as agreed and signed, but our expectations to be treated as an equal signatory was frustrated, which can be seen from this document. No reports that were sent from the OSCE mission to OSCE headquarters or any other parties were forwarded to the Yugoslav government, although that was an explicit obligation under the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vollebaek, at this meeting, complain to you about weapons in barracks or anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he only asked for helicopter weapons and a radio station?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: His requests were recorded faithfully, and I believe that he received the only possible reactions to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He required nothing else from you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please -- now please go to tab 27; Exhibit number 2D330. It's a decision of federal government, so please comment.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before each international visit, be it a visit of Yugoslav representatives to foreign countries or international organisations or visits of the representatives of foreign governments or international organisations to Yugoslavia, the federal government always defined its position with regard to that. These positions contained our objectives and the instructions for these talks. This is such a position which was being prepared on the occasion of the visit of Nikola Sainovic, a federal deputy prime minister to Sweden and he Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at item 3 on page 4. What did Mr. Sainovic have the authority to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we have this on e-court, because the document -- is the document simply this one page letter? I was expecting something lengthy, Mr. Fila. I think it's my mistake. Just please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is my mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Go to tab 28, please. The Exhibit number is 2D183. This is the proposal of the negotiating positions before that visit. Now please go to page 4, item 3, and what kind of talks did Mr. Sainovic -- was Mr. Sainovic going to have?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government precisely defined the framework in which Mr. Sainovic had the liberty to move on the occasion of his visit to foreign countries; and, in this case, the first objective set by government is condemning terrorism and putting the KLA on the list of terrorist organisations. There is no need for me to read out the rest, but what's most important is that our objective was to win over influential countries in the world, especially in Europe, to cut money lines and the lines of supply in terms of weapons for the terrorists. And this proposal was accepted by the Security Council, which in nearly all its resolutions and communiques demanded that all members of the UN stop the training, funding, and arming of the terrorist KLA. Moreover, the Security Council, in one of its resolutions, expressed a deep concern and sorrow that this is not fully respected by all UN members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now go to page 5, item B. What was Mr. Sainovic expected to do in accordance with government decisions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is also about his visit to two very influential European countries, EU members and members of the OSCE, which meant that we expected support for the renewal of our rights as members of international organisations, especially the OSCE, and he was supposed to ask his interlocutors in these two countries to deploy their contingents of inspectors in accordance with the agreement, Jovanovic-Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The purpose was the manning of the mission?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please go to tab 29.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a minute. Exhibit number is 2D228. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a protest lodged by the government of Yugoslavia. This protest note was sent to the Kosovo Verification Commission and to the OSCE in Vienna, and it's about certain incidents at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing, because certain equipment was found that wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No need to go through that. What did you believe the Kosovo Verification Mission had done by carrying weapons and goods that had not been declared and bringing them into the country?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We believed this constituted a violation of the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement, because items were found that were not in compliance or in keeping with the civilian and diplomatic character of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that constitute a violation of the Vienna Conventions, too?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, it did. There is no rule in international relations that allows diplomats to carry weapons or, indeed, the sort of equipment contrary to what should normally be the position of a diplomat or the civilian nature of their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just another thing: Was this the only such situation, or did this recur a number of times?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were several such situations that occurred. This is just a single incident. It's more of an example than the overall picture, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Go to tab 30, please; Defence Exhibit 2D217. Have you found it, sir? Tab 30. The document bears the date of the 13th of February, 1999, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to the introductory section of the document. Who is it that's arriving, what is this about, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the 13th of February was the time when negotiations were in progress to achieve a peaceful political solution. This was a time when public threats were made of armed aggression by NATO against Yugoslavia. This was also time of very intense terrorist activity over in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One can see that an official visit took place on the 9th and 10th of February; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, this is just one illustration of a whole series of political and diplomatic initiatives in progress in Belgrade at the time. This is a visit of the foreign minister of a friendly country. He was welcomed at the highest possible level. In addition to the president of Yugoslavia and the president of Serbia, he was also received by the president of the Assembly and even Deputy Prime Minister Vuk Draskovic. In Montenegro, he was received by the President of Montenegro. This clearly shows the sort of welcome that was extended by Yugoslavia to visiting foreign dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he was received by a number of different high-ranking state officials. Is this typical of the way Yugoslavia treated these visiting foreign dignitaries at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was no exception. It was more a rule, really. More or less, the same thing applied to Mr. Vollebaek's visit. It wasn't quite the same, but again he met everyone that he wanted to meet and talked to them, although the visit itself had been different because he came as the president of the OSCE. Well, this shows us Yugoslavia's commitment to use evolved diplomatic means an international dialogue to contribute to solving the problem of Kosovo and Metohija. Another thing that this document tells us is what the positions were of the Greek government. Fundamentally, they were identical to those expressed by the Yugoslav government, especially as far as a peaceful political solution was concerned, but also as far as the principles were concerned, the only principles that such a solution could possibly have been based on. As you can see, if you look at the document, Minister Pangalos expressed his full support of sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia. He was also in favour of a peaceful solution, and by no means in favour of a military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the fact that various domestic dignitaries were receiving those people; Milosevic and those in Montenegro, too? Does that show something that the atmosphere that prevailed among the Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how the system worked in both Serbia and Yugoslavia. That's how the political system worked. This is an expression of respect. This is also tantamount to compliance with the certain mechanical processes that cannot be restricted or exhausted by simply talking to individual foreign dignitaries. One must talk to all the representatives of all the relevant political agencies, institutions, and structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these institutions existed, and they did their job, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, Greece was at that time a member of NATO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: NATO decisions are taken unanimously, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a former minister of a country that was itself not a member of NATO, I'm not familiar with the decision-making process that applies to NATO countries. I believe you will find that easy enough to understand. However, I am deeply convinced that the positions expressed by Minister Pangalos during his visit to Yugoslavia were sincere, and in no way did these positions run counter to the inherent principles of Greece as a Balkan country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 3, the bottom of paragraph 3. This paragraph 3 on page 2 of the report itself in the English version. What is Greece's stated political position as far as the resolution of the Kosovo issue was concerned on the eve of the Rambouillet talks, in a manner of speaking, since the dates are the 9th and the 10th?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the positions of Serbia and Yugoslavia on the one hand, and those expressed by Greece often the other, quite regardless of the fact that Greece happened to be also a member of certain international organisations which Yugoslavia and Serbia at the time had no access to, were nevertheless quite close, and I believe they had remained that way. They were close if not essentially identical. Separatism in Kosovo and Metohija, and I hope that is beyond dispute, does not merely jeopardise the sovereignty and integrity of Serbia or what was at the time still Yugoslavia, but also those of other Balkan countries, including Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, we see the same fundamental political position espoused by Greece restated. What do they say about Kosmet and the border?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The dilemma I keep facing is this: Should I go to the substance of this document, Should I use it to back my words, or should I assume that the substance is familiar to everyone. It goes without saying that we see here the positions espoused by Greece: A political, peaceful solution for the Kosovo and Metohija, the need for dialogue, and the need for reasserting international borders plus autonomy for Kosovo and Metohija within the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In February 1999, despite the fact that they were a member of NATO, the Greek foreign minister put forward these positions that you have now elucidated for us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you go to paragraph 4 or item 4 halfway down the first paragraph. This was our position -- or rather, your position. The following sentence, Mr. Jovanovic, starts with "We repeated," and so on and so forth. Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1999, an important meeting of the Contact Group was held in London, establishing a set of ten principles to deal with Kosovo and Metohija. These principles were did not entirely take into account in the best possible way the interests of Serbia and Yugoslavia, despite which the Yugoslav government and the Serbian government decided to accept and recognise these ten principles. Throughout this entire process, the government advocated their implementation, and it stood up to any attempt to twist their meaning during the actual implementation and use them for something else. That was not in the spirit of the original principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to item 2 on page 6. This is the second paragraph on page 6 of the English. What is Pangalos saying there? What is he proposing for the FRY?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Minister Pangalos stated a very clear position here: Any negotiations on Kosovo and Metohija -- no negotiations on Kosovo and Metohija must lead to independence. He proposed that the Yugoslav government state this in no uncertain terms during the Rambouillet talks. On the other hand, Minister Pangalos expressed his unreserved support and understanding for Yugoslavia's efforts to renew it's membership rights in all international organisations, in which Yugoslavia at the time was suspended or its status was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the position on the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes without saying that Mr. Pangalos called for a suspension or abolition of all kinds of sanctions. If I may just remind you that the sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia by a Security Council decision back in 1992 were abolished by a Security Council resolution back in early 1996 after the successful conclusion of the Dayton-Paris Accords. Following that, some countries, and particularly the United States, kept what they referred to as an external wall, a barrier of sanctions. Although I have every respect for these countries, I must now say that those sanctions were illegal, simply because they were not in line with the previous resolution by the Security Council on abolishing the sanctions or lifting the sanctions. Likewise, other types of sanctions had been introduced. In our assessment, and as far as I can see in Mr. Pangalos's assessment as well, those sanctions were not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand. Were these sanctions imposed by the UN and the Security Council, or was this something done by the US of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time Security Council sanctions had been lifted, with the exception of the ban on importing weapons into the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have wrapped this up now, and let us open the Rambouillet chapter. Did the federal government had a role to play in the Rambouillet and Paris talks?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, minister -- I'm a former minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, once a minister, always a minister.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the government did have a role to play in the Paris-Rambouillet talks, as it did in the political discourse at the time, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who set the political platform for these talks?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The platform was set by the federal government; nevertheless, the platform had been closely coordinated with the government of the Republic of Serbia. There is one thing I wish to say. The international community remained adamant at all times that the problem of Kosovo and Metohija should be approached from the federal level rather than from the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what about the federal level? Who were the federal representatives at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government appointed two of its deputy prime ministers to participate in the talks; the first being Nikola Sainovic and the other being Professor Vladan Kutlesic. Sainovic was appointed because he was the person most privy to diplomacy and various international activities concerning the problem of Kosovo and Metohija. Further, he was the one with the greatest number of international contacts, and he was also the chairman for cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission. On top of this, he was the president of the foreign policy commission of the federal government. Dr. Vladan Kutlesic, on the other hand, was appointed because he was a scholar, a law expert, and had himself been involved in a number of different talks with the international players concerning Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the Foreign Ministry, or rather, you on his behalf? What about people from the Foreign Ministry? Did you provide the logistics to the Serbian delegation that was on its way to Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Foreign Ministry placed at the disposal of the Yugoslav Serbian state delegation in Rambouillet all of its professional technical and human resources, and I'm not just talking about the staff at our embassies in France. This also included a whole number of top-notch diplomats from some of the neighbouring countries; such as Switzerland, Belgium, and a number of other countries. In addition to this, a working group was dispatched from Belgrade, comprising top-notch professionals, lawyers, diplomats, and clerical staff, including no less than 20 persons. Throughout the talks, they remained at the disposal of our state delegation in both Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The mandate is generally known. We've looked at the Assembly decision a number of times, so it's not my intention to tire you with that now, sir, but let me phrase this differently. What was the only issue that our delegation at Rambouillet was unable to discuss?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The only issue that our delegation had no authority, power, or, indeed, ability to discuss was the territorial integrity of the country. All other aspects leading to a peaceful political solution were fair game, and they had carte blanche to negotiate all such elements; although, in all fact, no negotiations at all took place there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We'll get to at that later. Will you please go to tab 31. This is Defence Exhibit 1D18, page 414 in e-court, item 111. What is this about, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the ten principles of the Contact Group, which constitute a basis and a framework for a peaceful political solution for Kosovo and Metohija. As I've mentioned before, these were agreed at a meeting of the Contact Group that was held in London. You can see the date for yourself; the 30th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What follows is really important. Were these negotiable principles or non-negotiable principles to be accepted by each of the parties before the start of talks?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the positions stated by the Contact Group - and we know what its composition was - these were non-negotiable principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So we, as a country, were invited to negotiate based on these principles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Negotiations got off the ground - we've heard about that - but there's something else I want you to tell me now. Throughout the course of these talks, did you know that Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic ever came to Belgrade for the duration of the talks; although, the rule was that in one was to leave the castle premises? Did he do this at anytime; and if so, what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that Mr. Sainovic, at one point, came back to Belgrade during the actual talks. I spoke to him, as did Milosevic and Bulatovic. The Rambouillet talks had been bogged down. Our delegation had been asked to state its positions and to accept certain solutions that were not in keeping with the ten principles of the Contact Group. My understanding was Mr. Sainovic was in Belgrade, having previously received permission of the co-chairmen of the conference, or at least that's what he told me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the stumbling-block? Did our people actually sign those ten principles? Someone said at the request of Robin Cook, I'm not sure if that's true; whereas the, Albanians refused to signed the principles. Was that the stumbling-block?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is crystal clear that what was at stake here were the vital interests of the country. No aberration would have been allowed from the previously agreed platform that had been defined jointly by the government of Yugoslavia and the government of Serbia. There were emphatic attempts, however, to place our state delegation under pressure and force their hand to accept principles that were contrary to the ten principles of the Contact Group and that were, needless to say, contrary to the political platform envisaged for the talks. There was the danger that one might stray from these principles. Our state delegation came forward with the following initiative: They suggested that the ten indisputable principles be signed. The state delegation felt that this was some form of guarantee that the other sections of the agreement would be kept, more or less, within the limits of these ten principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What conclusion did you reach at those meetings? Did you decide that the talks should continue or halt? What did you do? What did you as a -- as the Foreign Minister do?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two conclusions that the talks should go ahead, and that the diplomats for their part should step up their activities at the international level in order to ensure support and understanding from influential international players, especially in terms of compliance with the ten principles set forth by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you receive any assurances that the matter would go no further?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is understood. None of our collocutors in any of these various international institutions spoke against the ten principles. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, was that the reason for Mr. Sainovic flying back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to tab 32 and look at P474. What sort of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
