utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm facing some technical difficulties here. I'm trying to turn this around. Are you talking about 542, 543, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tab 42. P474 is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is a document in English. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the text of the so-called provisional agreement on peace and self-determination in Kosovo, otherwise known as the Rambouillet agreement, dated the 23rd of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this the draft agreement that our delegation was asked to accept and sign?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is quite a voluminous document, and I can't now confirm that it contains everything, all the sections of the agreement, but I should assume so. And these were the demands made by the international players for the Serbian delegation to sign, the Yugoslav Serbian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before your arrival, this document was extensively discussed in this courtroom. I will ask you, Mr. Jovanovic, to comment on some provisions only. Please take a look at annex 7.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Give me the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is page 24, and in the book it's page 588. It is annex 7, and it also has a sub-annex B. Can you tell us what it says? Annex 7, supplement B, and on -- item 8.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that it is page 588 in the English version and item B?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Supplement B, item 8.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This text is very clear. It says that, "NATO troops, their staff or personnel, vessels, equipment," et cetera, "should be granted unlimited access and movement through all of Yugoslavia, including the right to use airspace and the territorial waters of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." In accordance with this, these provisions, NATO would be entitled to stay on the territory of -- of FRY and any part of its territory, without limitations in time or any other limitations. They would also have the right to hold military manoeuvres and exercises anywhere they wanted. They could also use any facility during the -- their entire stay in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With no limitation in time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were no limitations in time; no legal or constitutional limitations whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now go to page 68, item 5 in the English version, P474. It is page 24 in e-court, and it's page 589 in the book. Please take a look at item 15. What is -- what should NATO also be allowed to do in our country?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, in this item, you mentioned NATO shall be allowed, without limitations, to use the entire electromagnetic spectrum of Yugoslavia for their forces. I'm a layman when it comes to electromagnetic spectrum, but still I understand that to mean that the legal proprietors and users can be deprived of their rights to use part of the spectrum, including the army, the police, emergency services. So all of these would -- would be in a position to lose access to electromagnetic -- to portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, without -- without payment or without limitation in time, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please look -- go to page 25 in e-court or page 590 in the book. It's item 21. What powers is NATO accorded here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: NATO has no rights, but would like to have them. This item states that NATO shall be authorised to detain citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia without answering to anyone, which under international law is known as surrender, because when a foreign national in any country has greater rights than the citizens of that country, this is -- this is described as surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of such rights accorded to NATO anywhere else, to go about arresting people in England, Greece, or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes without saying that such demands are contrary to all, not only to all legal norms and standards, but also to all standards of contemporary civilisation, and that there is no sovereign country in the world where NATO has rights that come even close to these. And Yugoslav was exerted pressure -- was exerted pressure upon to sign or accept such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now go to page --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honours, I would like to add one sentence. Such provisions in this so-called Rambouillet agreement were in fact an ultimatum, and it was a demand to occupy all of Yugoslavia, not only part of it, and this is completely unacceptable. So all of Yugoslavia would -- would basically be occupied. So this text is a sad testimony of something that, in my opinion, should never have happened or be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does -- did any citizen of Yugoslavia under the constitution or any -- any legal act have the right to sign anything like this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Clearly, nobody had the right to sign such a humiliating document. Any educated person in the world is -- is able to come to the conclusion that no country in the world would under any circumstances possibly agree to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You remained in your position even after the fall of Milosevic for a certain time. Was such -- was this document ever offered or proposed to any subsequent government after Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please go to tab 33, Exhibit 2D221. What is this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the positions of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the so-called military presence [Realtime transcript read in error "prisons"], and this position was sent to the federal government by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on page 94, line 6, what is said here military "prisons," that's not what the witness said. He said military "presence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it clear, from this document, that NATO would enter only K and M, and only then would it go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be seen from this document that Yugoslav diplomacy reacted to statements in the media and elsewhere about the necessity to admit NATO military forces to Kosovo and Metohija. The ministry thought the time had come for -- for the clarification of this issue, and that's why it submitted these positions to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in the meantime, the demands -- the demands had been extended to an occupation of the entire country, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what is your opinion of the Rambouillet talks with regard to the ten basic principles of the Contact Group and onwards?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there were no real talks in Rambouillet. Anyway, that was a show, the purpose of which was to depict Serbia and the federal Republic of Croatia [as interpreted] as a -- as an uncooperative party. And these talks on Rambouillet were actually a pretext for the preparation of the aggression of NATO against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction of the transcript. It says Federal Republic of "Croatia," but it's actually Federal Republic of "Yugoslavia," with all due respect for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The documents that were put forward for signing could not be accepted, as you said. Then why were they offered to us at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have answered this question in part. An excuse was sought for the military campaign of NATO against Yugoslavia, and I can say that in some chapters of the so-called Rambouillet agreement or about some chapters there were no talks at all, no negotiations, nor were those chapters introduced in the negotiation process. And those were chapters 2, 5, and 7 of the agreement containing the very provisions about -- of a military and security character. So this so-called Rambouillet agreement was only disclosed to the Yugoslav Serbian side in small portions at once, and these are methods that are -- that are not used in serious talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go to tab 24, Exhibit number 2D241. Sorry, it is tab 34. Exhibit number 2D241. I'm referring to the last paragraph of page 6 of the English version and its continuation on page 7?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the reference to the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2 in the Serbian text. Please comment what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a very unusual, a very strange position put forward by Mr. Joschka Fischer, the German Minister of Foreign Affairs, who asked that Yugoslavia sign the agreement as a whole; because if they -- we failed to do so, it will have to negotiate directly with the USA, which will not end well for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In my opinion, this is a blunt and inappropriate threat of a highly esteemed European country against a smaller and weaker but still sovereign country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Van den Broek's position with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van den Broek was saying that this was Yugoslavia's last chance; and if this opportunity is missed, he announced a possible break-up of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It is unclear what he meant by the possible break-up, but it is possible that -- that such threats are uttered before an imminent aggression by NATO. It remains unclear why it would be dangerous, according to Mr. Fischer, if Yugoslavia were to negotiate with the USA. Does that mean that having talks with the most influential country in the world is dangerous per se?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Van den Broek say anything about minority rights here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van den Broek put forward an idea which is unheard-of in international relations and in the practice of international relations; namely, that a sovereign, independent country is expected to respect the right of an ethnic minority to self-determination. There is no such practice in international relations, because the Albanian minority at that time, and today still, has a country where the Albanians are a minority. That's Albania. And the ethnic Albanians in Serbia, in accordance with the framework convention of the Council of Europe, have the status of an ethnic minority in the ethnic -- sorry, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and now in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please go to tab 35 and take a look at Exhibit number 2D242. What is this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes from the -- from a session of the federal government when I informed the government of the results of the meetings concerning Kosovo and Metohija and Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the last page of the -- the announcement by the co-chairmen. This is the supplement. What does it say? What kind of document is this, and what is it about? You see that it's dated Paris, 19th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The co-chairmen of the meetings in Paris and Rambouillet stated on March 19th, among others, that negotiations are -- would be postponed, and that the meetings would not be continued unless the Serbs accept the agreements. I have already had the opportunity to state that there were no agreements in Paris or Rambouillet. There were texts but not agreements. And the sentence in this announcement of the co-chairmen, in other words, not the entire Contact Group, is in fact an ultimatum to Serbia and Yugoslavia. This is contradictory in itself because it says that talks would not continue unless the Serbs declared that they accept the agreements. Now the question is: Why continue talks if it is supposed and, in fact, what is demanded is that agreements are accepted? Because once agreements are accepted, there's no point in negotiating or continuing talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at item 4 - you've covered it already - and item 5.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: About item 4, I can say that this is an insinuation. The two co-chairmen in an inappropriate way state -- make statements here. It says "unless the Serbs declare." Which Serbs? We're talking about the state delegations of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And the text in parentheses here is probably meant to mean that the entire Contact Group agrees with this; whereas, it was very clear that the Russian representative and the Contact Group never accepted the entire text that was offered, nor did he sign it when the representatives of the political parties of the Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija did, and so did the representative of the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now take a look at item 5. What does the -- what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another threat against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia. It is somewhat differently phrased from the act order of NATO, but it's basically the same thing. It says: "Consultations with our partners and allies will start in order to be ready to act." Will they also consult Russia as a partner, we could ask, or are everybody else partners except for some members of the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. But there's also item 6: "Warning the authorities in Belgrade not to launch any military offensive in the field and not to prevent, in any way, the personal freedom of movement and the activities of the KVM." Would this be a breach of obligations agreed to? How does this fit into the context of a bombing or is this a pretext also?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that this -- what kind of games, inappropriate games, are played at high levels. The decision of withdrawing the mission from Kosovo and Metohija is presented as a measure, the objective of which is their security and safety. But there was no reason for such warnings, because even though there was an overt threat of aggression against Serbia and Yugoslavia, there had been no measures on the -- that would jeopardise the security of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: These were stated by Mr. Cook and his colleague?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The KVM was able to move about Kosovo without any difficulties and without any danger from the side of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the signatories of this document are Mr. Hubert Vedrine and Mr. Cook; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This brings us to the end of this topic. We're about to broach our last topic. Do you know anything about Mr. Nikola Sainovic's activities after the outbreak of war in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What exactly do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since the beginning of NATO's aggression, Mr. Nikola Sainovic had the important task of establishing, developing, and promoting a dialogue with Ibrahim Rugova, who was the most well-liked and respected politician from the Albanian ranks in Serbia. He did establish dialogue, which was in itself a highly complex and arduous task. Rugova himself had reason to be reserved about any such initiatives given the extremism that was rife in the environment in which he lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you date these activities for us, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think this happened sometime in April 1999, amid NATO's aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that is perhaps early May 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite likely. I don't remember the specific date, but there must be documents showing the exact dates, and I don't think anyone's challenged those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know if he went back after this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nikola Sainovic, in a way, had experience in international dialogue and international relations, generally speaking; but, originally, he is an economist. He comes from East Serbia and, originally, he was a well-respected economist. Throughout the aggression, he was helping with protecting and relocating certain facilities and factories that were dangerous to their environment or that were potentially dangerous if they were bombed or targeted, and that could have possibly led to even greater disasters than those originally caused by the aggression itself, and that was why he was put in charge of these jobs. It is self-explanatory that this was both necessary and useful. I know that he was involved in protecting the Baric chemical plant near Belgrade and some other plant as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 36 and look at 2D365.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Briefly, what was this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There. I wasn't wrong. The meeting took place on the 5th of April. Nikola Sainovic and Ibrahim Rugova met in Pristina. They agreed on two points.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We can all read that.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That there should be a political process to resolve the problems, and that one had to work together to bring back refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please go to tab 37, document 1D36. This is an announcement or a communique. Please comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a joint statement by the federal government and the government of the Republic of Serbia, the interesting thing being it was adopted at two separate meetings or sessions. This is based on Milosevic's and Sainovic's meetings with Ibrahim Rugova. What we see here is the two essential principles being repeated: The need for a political agreement and the need for return of political refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is not the demand made here that one should start a dialogue, and so on and so forth. Well, that's all right, I suppose. Let's leave it at this. It says what it says. We can all read it for ourselves. Mr. Jovanovic, based on what you know and based on your close cooperation with Mr. Sainovic in terms of your work, international relation, and everything else you've been talking about, did you ever find out that Sainovic, in any way, throughout NATO's aggression was in any way involved in organising the defence forces in Kosovo and Metohija, be it army or police?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you think he could possibly have had the time to do anything like that given his numerous other tasks and his involvement elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've talked about that. It's self-explanatory, isn't it? We did say that, for a while, Sainovic had more to do in terms of international relations; but when NATO's aggression began, his duty was to open, promote, and develop political dialogue with the Albanian side, first and foremost, with Ibrahim Rugova. The documents clearly show that he was indeed successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To deal with the consequences.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to deal with the consequences and to protect the plants, which if targeted might have caused disasters that were nearly unfathomable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My next question: Throughout 1998 and 1999, do you ever hear of the term "Joint Command" being used or, indeed, later?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about later when the indictments was being published, did you hear that term being used?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The only time I came across the term was in the actual indictment and after the trial here before this Court here got underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about your information about the functioning of the army of Yugoslavia? Did they keep within the chain of command? Were there any interferences, any complaints, any objections being raised about this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the government, and I was in charge of foreign relations which was specific area. I attended a great number of meetings before NATO's aggression, during NATO's aggression, and after. My assessment is unequivocal. All the constituent elements of the constitutional system acted in a harmonised way and perfectly in keeping with the constitution and the law. The degree of efficiency displayed in our defence against NATO would have otherwise been impossible. The aggression lasted for as long as 80 days. This would not have been possible had not all of the country's elements been active and had they all not played their role successfully in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question to you, and let me please express my gratitude for you having to come to testify in my case, something about Sainovic's political views on Kosovo and Metohija: What were his political views on Kosovo and Metohija throughout the years that he spent working with you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I think your question is superfluous. It should be crystal clear, based on everything I am saying today, that Mr. Sainovic was always in favour of dialogue, in favour of a peaceful political solution, in favour of a solution that would above all preserve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country, yet at the same time would secure the highest possible level of self-government for the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija. Throughout our years of cooperation, I never once noticed a single aberration on his part from this constructive political position that he always espoused, which is respect for all citizens of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as all having equal rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Dealing with exhibits, I think you've taken us to Exhibit 37, and then there are another six.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are documents for the next witness. We'll be using these documents with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And two, I think, have not -- two of the earlier ones have not been referred to specifically in the course of the presentation. Number 7, which is 2D78, but I think it simply is a cover for number 8; is that correct? So if it hasn't been admitted already, it can be admitted on that basis. And number 27, there was some confusion, I think at that stage in the evidence. It turned out you were, in fact, referring to number 28, and we did deal with 28. And it may be that 27 is simply a supplement to 28 and can be admitted on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic is about to explain this. I'm sure he's better able than I am to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, tab 2D78, this is the agenda containing the proposed agreement that the witness mentioned. This is a separate document showing what the procedural aspects were of adopting the agreement that the witness mentioned. It is an entirely autonomous document in relation to tab 8, P432, which is the text of the agreement itself. This is -- the previous document is more by way of an explanation to explain the procedure that the federal government adopted for this agreement that the witness later signed with the Polish Foreign Minister, Mr. Geremek. I'm talking about 2D78. May that please be admitted as a separate document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And then what about 2D330? That's tab 27.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Petrovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D330, tab 27, this is about the decision of the federal government about a meeting that was held on the 14th of January, where the principles were set out for Mr. Sainovic's talks. The principles or the outline can be found at tab 28. This is 2D183. Again, we are looking at two separate documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tab 27 can be admitted, that is 2D330, in light of its association with tab 28. The document in French, which was tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just going to tell you that that will be admitted, not marked for identification. It was adequately presented and doesn't need further translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's clear that all of these exhibits in the binder up to number 36 -- or to 37, I think, are admitted. Well, I gather our sitting tomorrow will be confined to the morning; therefore, from 9.00 until 1.45. It's not proved possible to make any other arrangement. Mr. Jovanovic, we have to terminate our proceedings for today at this stage, and we will continue tomorrow at 9.00, so you have to be back here ready to recommence at 9.00. As I say to every witness who comes here in that situation, you must have no communication whatsoever with any person about the evidence, either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give. There is no barrier on you communicating with anyone you like about whatever you like as long as you do not overnight and before returning here discuss any aspect of the evidence. Now, would you please leave the courtroom in the company of the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
